result:
The kettle is louder than it used to be, or maybe I'm just less used to hearing it alone. It that whine that starts low and sympathetic, like a cat stretching on a windowsill, before it becomes a shriek that makes your teeth ache. I lift the lid. Steam pours out in a thick white curtain that smells faintly of the plastic filter I put in last month, which is a smell I will never be able to name but that I will remember in ten years when I'm in a car on a highway and the road ahead is empty and the dashboard clock says 6:47 and I realize I am exactly here and exactly now and the fact of it makes me want to cry in a way that feels almost stupid.

I pour the water into the mug. The mug is the blue one, the one with a chip on the rim where I dropped it on the kitchen tile three weeks ago. I could have thrown it out. I did not throw it out. I set it in the drying rack and it dried and I picked it up the next morning and it was still chipped. There is a kind of loyalty in that that I find both tender and slightly alarming, like a friendship that has been left unchallenged for so long you're not sure you still like the person, but now you just can't imagine not sitting next to them at the kitchen table on a Tuesday.

Tuesday. That word still feels strange, even now. It is the second day. It is not a beginning and not an ending. It is the day that has already decided what it is before you get out of bed. I think about how we build our entire emotional architecture around Mondays—Mondays as the great reset, the great whiteboard we erase and draw on fresh—and yet by Tuesday the eraser is worn thin and the chalk dust is in our hair and the fresh drawing looks like a smudge. And no one notices the smudge. They just pick up the pencil and make a line in the smudge and call it the outline of a person.

Outside the window the neighbor is walking a dog that is very small and very angry at everything. A leaf, a bird, the particular angle at which a parking lot pole meets the asphalt. The dog's owner walks with that patient, slightly amused limp, the kind of face that says *yes, yes, he hates the universe, I'm aware, please proceed.* I watch them go around the block and disappear behind the row of houses and the feeling I get is not quite sad. It is the feeling of watching a thing happen and knowing, with a quiet and absolute certainty, that I will not see it again in that exact configuration. The dog will grow or die or the owner will move or the leaf will turn to another leaf. The streetlight will flicker the same way it did the day I noticed it flickering, and I will not notice. This is not a tragedy. This is just Tuesday.

I stand at the counter in my undershirt and I think about how the concept of "a morning" is so impossibly specific. There is no morning. There is only this: the particular quality of light hitting the counter at an angle that makes the scar from when I cut myself on a jar lid in 2019 look like a small silver lake. The sound of the refrigerator doing its thing, that low electrical hum that is so constant you stop hearing it and then, for three seconds, you hear it, and the hearing of it is like hearing your own name spoken from across a crowded room. The fact that my left foot is colder than my right foot. The fact that I had a dream last night about a door in a hallway and I walked through it and it opened onto a kitchen I recognized but could not place, and the kitchen was full of people eating something I could see but not taste, and I was very calm about it, like walking into a room where you know you're expected.

I drink the tea. It is green tea, the kind that tastes like a green leaf has been heated gently and is slowly, resentfully, giving up its flavor. I hold the mug with both hands. My thumbs find the chip. The chip catches. There is a small, cold bite of it against my skin, and I think: this is the whole thing. This is the whole thing. The chip. The hum. The light on the scar. The dog on the other side of the street. The dream of the kitchen. None of it is a metaphor. I do not need to make it one. It is just happening, and it is specific, and it is mine, and it is already going.

And that is enough. I have been trying, for the last several years, to make it into something else. To turn the morning into a metaphor for mortality. To turn the chipped mug into a parable. To turn the green tea into a statement. And the thing is, I keep reaching for the frame, for the story, for the sentence that will make it *mean* something to someone else, in the way I am supposed to mean something. And the moment I reach for it, the thing I'm holding in my hands goes quiet, because it was never meant to be held up to the light and explained. It is meant to be hot. It is meant to be Tuesday. It is meant to be the exact temperature of a morning where you are alone and the neighbor's dog is still walking around the block and the kettle is still in the cabinet and it will be needed again.

I set the mug down. The chip scrapes the tile. A small sound. No one is here to hear it. The light is moving a little, just a little, across the counter. The refrigerator hums. I take a second sip of the tea. It is still hot. It is not yet good. It is getting close to good.

I do not know what I will write after this. I do not know if there is a next paragraph or if this is the whole of it. The page does not ask me. The morning does not ask me. The dog is still walking around the block, angry at the pole, and the owner is still walking with that patient, amused limp, and the leaf is still a leaf, and the streetlight will flicker tomorrow the same way it flickered today, and no one will be here to notice, which is fine, which is the whole point, which is the thing that makes it real.

I wash the mug. I dry it with the towel that has a small brown stain on the corner. I put it in the rack. It will dry. Tomorrow I will use the blue mug again. The chip will be there. The scar on the counter will catch the light at an angle I cannot predict. The tea will taste like a green leaf, resentfully giving up.

And I will be here. Exactly here. Exactly this Tuesday. In the exact configuration I will never see again.

And that will be enough. That will be the whole of it.
